1.title: Persistent and Ephemeral Volumes
1.text: Welcome to Module four: Persistent and Ephemeral Volumes. It covers the exam area Application Design and Build. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Two kinds of volume. Ephemeral volumes. host path. Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. Practice with five hands-on labs worth thirty-one points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Design and Build (twenty percent). Practice in this module: five labs, thirty-one points, about thirty-five minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: Two kinds of volume
1.text: Two kinds of volume. The figure shows this: Ephemeral and persistent volumes. Exam tip: An empty dir lives and dies with the Pod; use a Persistent Volume Claim for data that must survive.

1.title: Two kinds of volume, continued
1.text: Two kinds of volume. A container's own file system is thrown away when the container restarts. A volume is a directory that is mounted into one or more containers of a Pod, in two steps: the Pod lists it under spec dot volumes, and each container that wants it lists it under volume Mounts with a mount Path. Ephemeral. Examples: empty dir, config Map, secret, projected, downward A P I. Lifetime: the Pod's life: gone when the Pod is deleted. Persistent. Examples: persistent Volume Claim (P V or P V C (Persistent Volume Claim)), host path for a single node. Lifetime: beyond the Pod: the data stays.

1.title: Two kinds of volume, continued
1.text: Two kinds of volume. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Ephemeral volumes
1.text: Ephemeral volumes. empty dir. scratch space created empty when the Pod starts, shared by its containers; survives a container restart but not the Pod's deletion. empty dir with medium Memory. a R A M-backed T M P F S; counts against the container's memory; fast. empty dir with size Limit. the Pod is evicted if it uses more. config Map, secret. configuration files and credentials as files (Module nine). downward A P I. the Pod's own name, labels, limits as files. projected. several sources (Config Map, Secret, token, downward A P I) in one directory.

1.title: Ephemeral volumes, continued
1.text: Ephemeral volumes. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: hostPath (and why it is rarely right)
1.text: host path (and why it is rarely right). A host path volume mounts a directory of the node. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study. Exam tip: A host path volume keeps data on one node only, so use it only when a task asks for it.

1.title: hostPath (and why it is rarely right), continued
1.text: host path (and why it is rarely right). The data stays on that node only. If the Pod moves to another node, it sees a different directory. It also exposes the node's file system, so security rules often forbid it. Use it for node-level agents and for exam tasks that ask for it; use a Persistent Volume Claim for application data.

1.title: Persistent volumes, claims and StorageClasses
1.text: Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. The figure shows this: Persistent Volume, claim and Storage Class. Exam tip: A claim binds to a volume with the same storage Class Name, enough size and a compatible access mode.

1.title: Persistent volumes, claims and StorageClasses, continued
1.text: Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. Persistent Volume (P V). Who creates it: an administrator, or a provisioner. What it is: a piece of storage; cluster-wide (no namespace). Persistent Volume Claim (P V C). Who creates it: the developer. What it is: a request for storage of a size and access mode; namespaced. Storage Class. Who creates it: an administrator. What it is: a recipe for creating P V s on demand ("dynamic provisioning"). Binding. A claim binds to a P V (Persistent Volume) that has enough capacity, a compatible access mode and the same storage Class Name. Once bound, they belong to each other (the P V shows Bound and a claim Ref ). A Pod then mounts the claim, not the volume.

1.title: Persistent volumes, claims and StorageClasses, continued
1.text: Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. Read Write Once. Short: R W O (Read Write Once). Meaning: read-write by one node. Read Only Many. Short: R O X. Meaning: read-only by many nodes. Read Write Many. Short: R W X (Read Write Many). Meaning: read-write by many nodes. Read Write Once Pod. Short: R W O P. Meaning: read-write by one Pod. Retain. the P V and its data are kept; it is Released and must be cleaned by hand. Delete. the P V and the storage are deleted (the default for dynamic volumes). Static provisioning (an administrator creates the P V).

1.title: Persistent volumes, claims and StorageClasses, continued
1.text: Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Persistent volumes, claims and StorageClasses, continued
1.text: Persistent volumes, claims and Storage Classes. Dynamic provisioning (no P V is written by hand): omit storage Class Name to get the cluster's default Storage Class (marked default in kube control get sc ), or name a class. The provisioner creates the P V when the claim is used. On this test cluster the class standard (local-path) uses Wait For First Consumer: the claim stays Pending until a Pod uses it, and that is normal, not an error. Using the claim in a Pod.

1.title: Common failures
1.text: Common failures. P V C Pending, event says storage class not found. Cause: storage Class Name names a class that does not exist. Fix: recreate the P V C with a real class or none ( storage Class Name cannot be edited). P V C Pending, no P V matches. Cause: size, access mode or class mismatch with every P V. Fix: fix the claim or the P V. P V C Pending with Wait For First Consumer. Cause: no Pod uses it yet. Fix: create the Pod. Pod Pending, "unbound immediate Persistent Volume Claims". Cause: the claim is not bound. Fix: fix the claim first. Data gone after deleting the Pod. Cause: the data was on an empty dir. Fix: use a P V C. Exam tip: A claim that stays Pending has its reason in kube control describe pvc; with Wait For First Consumer it waits for a Pod.

1.title: Common failures, continued
1.text: Common failures. You can add a P V C to a Deployment the same way, but a Read Write Once volume can be mounted from one node at a time: several replicas on different nodes will not all start. A Stateful Set gives each replica its own claim with volume Claim Templates. Exam tip. To make a claim bind to a specific P V in a task, give both the same storage Class Name and a compatible size and mode. A claim without a class gets the default class and will not bind to a P V whose class is manual. Exam tip. kube control get pv,pvc dash A shows the whole picture; kube control describe pvc name has the reason in its events.

1.title: Lab 4.1: emptydir memory
1.text: Lab four point one: emptydir memory. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace vol, create a Pod named scratch with one container (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that has an ephemeral volume named cache mounted at slash cache. The volume must live in memory ( medium Memory ) and be limited to sixty-four mebibytes. Wait until the Pod is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 4.1: emptydir memory, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n vol apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

1.title: Lab 4.1: emptydir memory, Solution, continued
1.text: Lab four point one: emptydir memory, Solution, continued. Run empty dir. Then medium Memory. Then size Limit sixty-four mebibytes. Then Y. Then kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash scratch the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n vol exec scratch then the command df slash cache.

1.title: Lab 4.2: hostpath
1.text: Lab four point two: hostpath. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace vol, create a Pod named hp (image busy box one dot thirty-six ) whose container runs sh dash c echo hello from pod slash host data slash hello dot txt sleep three thousand six hundred. Mount the node directory slash opt slash C K A D data (create it if it does not exist, type Directory Or Create ) with a host path volume at slash host data in the container. The file must appear in slash opt slash C K A D data on the node that runs the Pod. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 4.2: hostpath, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n vol apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 4.2: hostpath, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point two: hostpath, Solution, continued. Run kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash hp the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then sleep three. Then node kube control dash n vol get pod hp dash o json path dot spec dot node name. Then docker exec node cat slash opt slash C K A D data slash hello dot txt.

2.title: Lab 4.3: pv pvc static
2.text: Lab four point three: pv pvc static. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. Create a Persistent Volume named pv reports (capacity two gibibytes, access mode Read Write Once, storage Class Name manual, reclaim policy Retain, host path slash mnt slash reports ). In the namespace vol, create a Persistent Volume Claim named pvc reports that requests one gibibyte with Read Write Once and storage Class Name manual, and a Pod named reporter (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that mounts the claim at slash reports. The claim must be bound to pv reports and the Pod Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 4.3: pv pvc static, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 4.3: pv pvc static, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point three: pv pvc static, Solution, continued. Run ---. Then api Version version one. Then kind Persistent Volume Claim. Then metadata. Then name pvc reports. Then namespace vol. Then spec. Then access Modes Read Write Once. Then storage Class Name manual. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Lab 4.3: pv pvc static, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point three: pv pvc static, Solution, continued. Run ---. Then api Version version one. Then kind Pod. Then metadata. Then name reporter. Then namespace vol. Then spec. Then containers. Then - name main. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Lab 4.3: pv pvc static, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point three: pv pvc static, Solution, continued. Run - name reports. Then persistent Volume Claim. Then claim Name pvc reports. Then Y. Then kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash reporter the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n vol get pvc.

2.title: Lab 4.4: dynamic pvc persists
2.text: Lab four point four: dynamic pvc persists. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace vol, create a Persistent Volume Claim named data that requests one gibibyte with Read Write Once from the cluster's default Storage Class (do not name a class). Create a Pod writer (image busy box one dot thirty-six ) that mounts it at slash data and runs sh dash c echo kept after delete slash data slash note dot txt sleep three thousand six hundred. When the file exists, delete the Pod writer and create a Pod reader (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that mounts the same claim at slash data. The file must still be there. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 4.4: dynamic pvc persists, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n vol apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 4.4: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point four: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued. Run ---. Then api Version version one. Then kind Pod. Then metadata. Then name writer. Then spec. Then containers. Then - name main. Then image busy box one dot thirty-six. The remaining lines are on the screen.

2.title: Lab 4.4: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point four: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued. Run kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash writer the timeout flag set to one hundred eighty seconds. Then sleep three. Then kube control dash n vol delete pod writer the wait flag set to true. kube control dash n vol apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen.

2.title: Lab 4.4: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued
2.text: Lab four point four: dynamic pvc persists, Solution, continued. Run - name store, mount Path slash data. Then volumes. Then - name store. Then persistent Volume Claim. Then claim Name data. Then Y. Then kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash reader the timeout flag set to one hundred eighty seconds. Then kube control dash n vol exec reader then the command cat slash data slash note dot txt.

2.title: Lab 4.5: fix pending pvc
2.text: Lab four point five: fix pending pvc. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace vol, the Pod db is Pending because its Persistent Volume Claim db data cannot be bound (the manifest is about slash work slash db dot yaml ). Fix the problem so that the claim is bound by the cluster's default Storage Class and the Pod is Running. Keep the names, the size ( one gibibyte ) and the access mode ( Read Write Once ). Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 4.5: fix pending pvc, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n vol describe pvc db data then pipe to tail -five. Then kube control get storageclass. Then kube control delete dash f about slash work slash db dot yaml the wait flag set to true. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then kube control apply dash f about slash work slash db dot yaml. Then kube control dash n vol wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash db the timeout flag set to one hundred eighty seconds. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the difference between empty dir and a Persistent Volume Claim? Answer: An empty dir lives and dies with the Pod; a claim's data outlives the Pod. Question two. What does medium Memory do on an empty dir? Answer: It makes the volume a R A M-backed T M P F S. Question three. When does a P V C bind to a P V? Answer: When the P V has enough capacity, a compatible access mode and the same storage Class Name.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. What does the Retain reclaim policy do? Answer: It keeps the P V and its data after the claim is deleted. Question five. What happens if a P V C omits storage Class Name? Answer: It uses the cluster's default Storage Class. Question six. Why is a claim Pending with the Wait For First Consumer binding mode? Answer: It waits until a Pod uses it; that is normal.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. Which access mode allows read-write from one node only? Answer: Read Write Once. Question eight. Can you change storage Class Name on an existing P V C? Answer: No; delete the claim and create it again.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Mount: volumes in the Pod, volume Mounts plus mount Path in the container. Ephemeral: empty dir ( medium Memory, size Limit ), config Map, secret, projected. host path: node directory; type Directory Or Create; data stays on that node. P V or P V C or class: P V cluster-wide, P V C namespaced, Storage Class makes P V s on demand. Bind rule: capacity, access mode and storage Class Name must fit. Access modes: R W O, R O X, R W X, R W O P. Reclaim: Retain keeps data; Delete removes the volume. Pending P V C: describe pvc events; wrong class; no consumer yet.
